# License of the content and the data

Three different things live in this repository, and they are not under one
license.

## The code — MIT

Everything under `src/`, `scripts/`, `tests/` and the configuration files. See
[LICENSE](LICENSE).

## The catalog and the editorial prose — CC BY 4.0

Everything under `data/canonical/`, the source manifests in `data/sources/`, the
methodology and preset texts in `src/content/`, the documents in `docs/`, and
the published exports built from them:

- `/data/catalog-v1.json`
- `/data/catalog-summary-v1.json`
- `/data/measurements-v1.csv`

These are licensed under the
[Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
You may share and adapt them, including commercially, provided you give
appropriate credit ("RetroFlops", with a link to
<https://github.com/retroflops/retroflops>) and say whether you changed
anything.

Individual facts are not copyrightable in most jurisdictions, and this license
does not claim otherwise. What it covers is the compilation: which machines were
chosen, which figures were judged acceptable, how they were normalized and
grouped, and the prose that explains all of it.

## The cited documents — their publishers'

Every figure in the catalog comes from a document somebody else wrote, and
nothing here grants any right over those documents.

- Each record in `data/sources/` states the license its publisher applies, in
  its `license` field, and any constraint that travels with a quotation in
  `usageNote`. Both are shown on the source's page on the site.
- **32 of the 38 sources are tier A**, mostly vendor documentation and technical
  manuals: they are quoted, not republished. Where an extract appears, in a
  research record or beside a figure, it is short and exists so a reader can
  check the number against its source.
- **NASA documents are public domain** as works of the United States Government,
  and are the only sources here with no restriction at all.
- **SPEC results carry the
  [SPEC Fair Use Rules](https://www.spec.org/products/fairuse/)**, which travel
  with the figure wherever it appears; the `usageNote` on those records is what
  puts the notice next to the number.
- **One source states no license at all** — Netlib's Dhrystone performance
  database, which has no governing body and publishes no terms. Its record says
  so rather than assuming a permission nobody granted.

If you are the rights holder of a cited document and something here overreaches,
open an issue: the figure will be re-sourced or removed, and the reasoning
recorded.

## Redistributing the exports

The exports carry no timestamp and no build identifier, so a copy can be
verified byte for byte against a build of the same records. Redistribute them
under CC BY 4.0 with attribution, and keep the source records with them: a
figure without its citation is exactly what this project exists not to publish.

  {{measurement:apple-m1:process-node}} die carrying processor cores, graphics

  clock frequency.
notes:
  The {{context:apple-m1:context-unit-8}} cores are four performance cores and
  four efficiency cores, so "eight cores" describes two different things counted
  together and no per-core figure would mean the same for both halves. The
  transistor count and the process node are recorded here because the catalog's
  metrics allow only `cpu` and `gpu` scope for them, but they belong to the
  whole die, graphics and neural engine included; both figures say so in their
  caveats.

name: MIPS R10000
manufacturer: MIPS Technologies

summary: >-

  R10010 Floating Point Chip", which is how SGI reported the on-die FPU
  revision. Caches in the Octane configurations recorded here are
  {{context:mips-r10000:context-kb-32}} instruction plus
  {{context:mips-r10000:context-kb-32}} data on chip, with
  {{context:mips-r10000:context-mb-1}} of unified secondary cache.

id: mos-6510
slug: mos-6510
kind: cpu
name: MOS Technology 6510
manufacturer: MOS Technology
architecture: MOS 6502
introducedDate: '1982'
instructionSet: MOS 6502
instructionSetFamily: mos-6502
summary:
  A 6502 with an on-chip eight-bit bidirectional I/O port. Internally identical
  to the 6502 for software compatibility; the extra port is what lets the
  Commodore 64 bank ROM and I/O in and out of a
  {{context:mos-6510:context-bit-16}} address space.
notes:
  56 instructions, thirteen addressing modes, decimal and binary arithmetic, an
  eight-bit data bus and a sixteen-bit address bus. The part is rated for
  {{context:mos-6510:context-mhz-1}} and {{context:mos-6510:context-mhz-2}}
  operation, which is a speed grade rather than the rate any particular machine
  clocks it at.
sourceIds:

editorialStatus: approved

  register width alone describes it poorly. The address space is larger than the
  memory fitted to the Amiga models in this catalog. Floating point is not on
  the die; it needs a 68881 or 68882 coprocessor.

id: motorola-68ec020
slug: motorola-68ec020
kind: cpu
name: Motorola MC68EC020
manufacturer: Motorola
architecture: Motorola 68020
introducedDate: '1991'
instructionSet: Motorola 68020
instructionSetFamily: motorola-68000
summary:
  'The cost-reduced 68020: a full {{context:motorola-68ec020:context-bit-32}}
  data path with the address bus cut to
  {{context:motorola-68ec020:context-bit-24}} and the memory management unit
  left out. The processor of the Amiga 1200.'
notes:
  Against the 68000 in the Amiga 500 it is a genuine generational change rather
  than a faster clock — a {{context:motorola-68ec020:context-bit-32}} data path
  instead of 16, an instruction cache, and single-access operations where the
  68000 needed two. Floating point is not on the die; the Amiga 1200 has a
  socket for a factory-installed 68881 or 68882 and nothing in it by default.
sourceIds:
  - amiga-1200-service-manual
editorialStatus: approved

id: amiga-ocs
slug: amiga-ocs
kind: gpu
name: Amiga Original Chip Set (Agnus and Denise)
manufacturer: Commodore-Amiga, Inc.
architecture: Amiga OCS
introducedDate: '1985'
summary:

  the copper display coprocessor and arbitrates memory; Denise generates the
  display and the sprites. Both work directly on Chip memory without involving
  the CPU.
notes:
  Paula, the third custom chip, handles audio and I/O and is not modeled here
  because the catalog records processors, graphics and memory only. The original
  Agnus reached 512K of Chip memory; Fat Agnus and later the Enhanced Chip Set
  raised that to {{context:amiga-ocs:context-mb-1}} and

name: MOS Technology VIC-II (6566/6567/6569)
manufacturer: MOS Technology
architecture: VIC-II
introducedDate: '1982'
summary:

  machine runs at whatever the video standard divides down to. It generates the
  display, fetches its own data from memory and drives the sprites Commodore
  called movable object blocks."
notes:
  The 6566 has thirteen fully decoded addresses for a static bus; the 6567
  multiplexes them for direct connection to 64K dynamic RAM. The 6569 is the PAL
  part. Bus mastering during raster fetches steals cycles from the processor, so
  the two chips share the memory bus rather than running independently.

id: apple-mac-mini-m1
slug: apple-mac-mini-m1
name: Apple Mac mini (M1, 2020)
manufacturer: Apple
type: personal-computer
family: apple-macintosh
releaseDate: 2020-11
region: Worldwide
summary: >-
  {{measurement:apple-m1:transistor-count}} on
  {{measurement:apple-m1:process-node}}, with processor and graphics cores
  sharing {{measurement:apple-mac-mini-m1:8gb:memory-capacity}} or
  {{measurement:apple-mac-mini-m1:16gb:memory-capacity}} of unified memory. The
  computer is rated at
  {{measurement:apple-mac-mini-m1:rated-power-consumption}}. Its performance and
  efficiency cores retain separate clock records.
description: >-
  This record continues a line the catalog has drawn since the Apollo Guidance
  Computer. The oldest machines here are described almost entirely by time: a
  memory cycle in microseconds, an addition in milliseconds. Home computers are
  described by frequency. Consoles add floating-point rates beside the
  frequency, then stop giving the frequency. The M1 has separate clocks for its
  performance and efficiency cores, rather than one CPU-wide rate.


  Apple gives a transistor count, a process node, a core count split into two
  kinds of core, and a graphics throughput figure. Only the first two are
  properly comparable with anything else in the catalog. A process node can be
  displayed, but node names stopped being physical dimensions long before this
  one, so the metric forbids ratios between them.


  The memory is unified, as the PlayStation 4's is, and fitted at manufacture.
  Two configurations were sold, {{context:apple-mac-mini-m1:context-gib-8}} and
  {{context:apple-mac-mini-m1:context-gib-16}}, and neither could be changed
  afterwards.
configurations:
  - id: 8gb
    label: 8 GB unified memory
    entries:
      - componentId: apple-m1
        role: main-cpu
        count: 1
        shared: false
        notes:
          Four performance cores and four efficiency cores with separate clock
          records.
        measurementIds:
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:cpu-clock-frequency-performance-cores
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:cpu-clock-frequency-efficiency-cores
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:cpu-clock-frequency
      - componentId: apple-m1-gpu
        role: gpu
        count: 1
        shared: false
        measurementIds:
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:gpu-clock-frequency
      - componentId: apple-m1-unified-memory
        role: unified-memory
        count: 1
        shared: true
        measurementIds:
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:8gb:memory-capacity
  - id: 16gb
    label: 16 GB unified memory
    entries:
      - componentId: apple-m1
        role: main-cpu
        count: 1
        shared: false
        notes:
          Four performance cores and four efficiency cores with separate clock
          records.
        measurementIds:
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:cpu-clock-frequency-performance-cores
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:cpu-clock-frequency-efficiency-cores
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:cpu-clock-frequency
      - componentId: apple-m1-gpu
        role: gpu
        count: 1
        shared: false
        measurementIds:
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:gpu-clock-frequency
      - componentId: apple-m1-unified-memory
        role: unified-memory
        count: 1
        shared: true
        measurementIds:
          - apple-mac-mini-m1:16gb:memory-capacity
notes: >-
  The release date is the date of the cited announcement. The Neural Engine's 11
  trillion operations per second is not recorded: the catalog has no metric for
  it, the operations are not floating-point, and inventing one for a single
  record would leave it comparable with nothing. Storage configurations are not
  recorded either. The catalog had no storage metric when this record was
  written, and it gained one with the iPhone. Filling this machine's in is a
  change for whoever next revisits it, not a side effect of another record. No
  derived claim compares this machine's graphics throughput with the PlayStation
  4's because both figures are provisional and they were obtained by different
  methods. The ratio formula would refuse it twice over.

id: dec-pdp-8
slug: dec-pdp-8
name: DEC PDP-8
aliases:
  - Straight-8
manufacturer: Digital Equipment Corporation
type: minicomputer
releaseDate: '1965'
region: United States
summary: >-
  The original table-model PDP-8 put a complete computer on a desk. Its standard
  system had {{measurement:dec-pdp-8:whole-system-memory-capacity}} of core
  memory, an operator console, and a Teletype. A direct-address addition took
  {{measurement:dec-pdp-8-processor:addition-time}}.
description: |-
  DEC offered the PDP-8 as a complete computer for calculation and control.
  This record covers the original table model with its standard processor,
  ferrite-core memory, operator console, and Model 33 ASR Teletype. Later PDP-8
  models and optional memory extension, arithmetic hardware, and CRT displays
  are outside this configuration.

  The Computer History Museum calls the PDP-8 the first commercially
  successful minicomputer. It contrasts the desk-sized machine and its lower
  price with a small IBM System/360, and credits that combination with bringing
  minicomputers into laboratories, offices, and industrial plants.

  Instructions and data share the fitted core, with
  {{context:dec-pdp-8-core-memory:word-width}} per word. The processor works
  through an accumulator and carry link. An instruction can directly address
  the first page of memory or the page it occupies; other pages need an
  indirect pointer. Separate instructions handle input/output and operations
  on processor registers. Auto-index registers help step through lists in
  memory. An interrupt sends a running program to a device-service routine;
  the separate data-break facility lets a peripheral transfer words directly
  to or from core through the memory buffer.

  The console switches let an operator load an address, deposit a word in core,
  examine memory, and advance a program by one cycle or instruction. The
  register lamps showed what the processor was doing. The Teletype accepted
  keyboard or paper-tape input and produced typed or punched output. DEC
  supplied a symbolic assembler that produced program tape, a FORTRAN compiler,
  a debugger, and a tape editor. Its Floating Point Package performed
  arithmetic in software.

  DEC specifies a {{context:dec-pdp-8-processor:computer-cycle-time}} computer
  cycle. Table 1 rates direct-address TAD (two's-complement add) at
  {{measurement:dec-pdp-8-processor:addition-time}}; indirect addressing adds
  another cycle. These timings do not establish a nominal processor clock.
configurations:
  - id: standard-table-model
    label: Original table model with standard core and Teletype ASR
    entries:
      - componentId: dec-pdp-8-processor
        role: main-cpu
        count: 1
        shared: false
        measurementIds:
          - dec-pdp-8-processor:clock-frequency
          - dec-pdp-8-processor:addition-time
          - dec-pdp-8-processor:peak-fp32-rate
      - componentId: dec-pdp-8-core-memory
        role: system-memory
        count: 1
        shared: false
        measurementIds:
          - dec-pdp-8-core-memory:capacity
          - dec-pdp-8:memory-bandwidth
    notes: >-
      The Teletype is part of DEC's standard installation but has no separate
      processor or memory component record. The cabinet photograph shows the
      console and enclosure, not the full installation.
sourceIds:
  - dec-pdp-8-high-speed-digital-computer-1965
  - chm-internet-history-1960s
imageIds:

editorialStatus: approved
notes: >-
  This is the original PDP-8, often called the Straight-8. Later machines with

summary: >-
  A microprogrammed System/360 mainframe, represented by the F50 configuration
  with {{measurement:ibm-2050f-main-storage:capacity}} of main storage.
description: |-
  IBM designed the Model 50 for commercial and scientific computing. Its
  universal instruction set combines the System/360 Standard, Commercial, and
  Scientific sets. The arithmetic unit handles decimal and hexadecimal
  arithmetic, including short and long hexadecimal floating-point operations.

  Read-only storage holds the microprogram that controls processor data flow;
  application programs cannot address it directly. Core main storage holds
  programs and data, while local storage holds registers and scratchpad data.
  Channels overlap input/output with processor work. The selected F50 configuration
  includes the processor's main storage without optional external core storage
  or a display unit.

  Software requirements depend on the operating system and release. IBM's DOS
  Release 24 manual specifies a minimum of
  {{context:ibm-system-360-model-50:dos-release-24-minimum-storage}} of main
  storage, below this configuration's
  {{measurement:ibm-2050f-main-storage:capacity}}. DOS also requires suitable
  disk equipment, which is not included here. The OS/360 MFT guide for Release
  21.7 requires at least
  {{context:ibm-system-360-model-50:mft-release-21-7-minimum-storage}} of main
  storage, exceeding this configuration's capacity. These later manuals
  describe software requirements, not the software supplied at introduction.

records.description: The A4000 moved the Amiga architecture into an expandable desktop case. Its stock processor module is a 68040. The CyberStorm configuration records a later accelerator that replaces that module with a 68060, so it belongs beside the standard configuration but is not presented as a Commodore shipping variant. The manual describes changeable Chip and Fast RAM rather than one fixed memory loadout.

records.description: Sinclair pushed almost everything outside the processor into a single custom chip, which is how the machine reached a price no rival matched. That chip also pauses the processor while it reads video memory, and the resulting contention is why one part of memory runs slower than the rest.
